newsitem.title: UK: European recovery may fuel, not hinder dollar rise.
newsitem.headline: European recovery may fuel, not hinder dollar rise.

text.p: Far from wincing at signs of European growth this year, the dollar may even thrive on it, some analysts argue.

Differences in spare economic capacity either side of the Atlantic, or the gap between between current and potential non-inflationary economic growth, means a rise in European activity could have very different exchange rate effects than currently expected, said analysts.
For much of 1996, dollar/mark's attempts to rally were often stymied by economic data from Germany and around Europe showing growth picking up in response to easy credit policies.

The rule of thumb for currency markets was that higher European growth would reverse the credit easing cycle too, forcing historically low rates in the core of Europe to rise and depressing the relative yield attraction of the dollar.
However, there are some analysts who say an acceleration of growth in Europe in 1997 may actually contribute to a sustained rise in the U.S. currency against its European counterparts.

Economic capacity constraints in the U.S. mean a pickup in European growth may finally force U.S. interest rates higher to prevent overheating and inflation. The extent of spare capacity in Europe, on the other hand, means growth can pick up there without raising the interest rate outlook to the same extent.
"The fear of the dollar being undermined by a European recovery is way overdone," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.

The rise of the dollar/mark rate to two-and-a-half year highs already this year has been driven primarily by a sharp widening of U.S. and European yield spreads in favour of the dollar on a perception of diverging economic trends.
However, the transmission mechanism between a European recovery and further dollar strength can work in three ways.
First, rising European growth should eventually feed through to domestic demand, suck more U.S. imports into Europe and help narrow the widening U.S. trade deficit with western Europe.
The trade gap between western Europe and the U.S., a source of concern for dollar bulls, has gone from a surplus in 1992 to a cumulative deficit in excess of $10 billion last year.

The deterioration in the bilateral U.S./Europe trade account is at least partly a reflection of feeble European economic activity and weak import demand rather than a fundamental imbalance in the dollar exchange rate.

"The relative cyclical strength of the U.S. economy is largely responsible for the deterioration of the U.S. trade deficit with Europe," said Prendergast. "If and when Europe recovers, we'll see at least some improvement in the trade gap."
Secondly, European growth could have the added stimulus of rising demand for U.S. exports, a squeeze on U.S. capacity constraints and ultimately higher interest rates.
"A generalised global economic recovery will make it more difficult for the Fed to hold off tightening this year," said Paul Meggyesi, currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Although the "European recovery/higher dollar' story may be too neat, a recovery could remove a safety valve for the Fed on interest rates, which in itself is good for the dollar."
The U.S. economy has been growing at a brisk clip in recent years, shrinking the unemployment rate there but failing to generate traditionally attendant inflationary pressures.
As a result, the U.S. Federal Reserve has left its key interest rates unchanged for almost a year despite forecasts throughoput 1996 that a rate rise was imminent.

However, a boost to U.S. exports from a rise in European growth may push U.S. capacity constraints into the danger zone and force the Fed to tighten credit by lifting short term interest rates and bolstering yield support for the currency.

In spite of higher growth, however, Europe would be loath to tighten credit for fear of choking its long sought-after recovery to death and will not want to undermine the dollar rally for which it has craved for so long. It will be even more reluctant to do so ahead of European monetary union in 1999.
Finally, the European recovery will help improve European exchequer revenues and enhance the fiscal tightening in place to help meet EMU budgetary targets on time.
Anything improving the chances of EMU going ahead on time, analysts argue, will only weaken the German mark further and accelerate the dollar/mark rally, analysts said.
